idiom_name: callables, closures and functools.partial as commands; a class with __call__ plus undo() for reversible actions
implementation_notes: In Python any callable already is a command: functions, bound methods, lambdas and the functools.partial objects the standard library describes as 'callable objects with some arguments pre-filled' are stored in a list and invoked later, so the common case needs no Command class at all. The classic structure survives in two narrow situations - a request that must expose an inverse (implement __call__ plus undo() on a small class, or keep a (do, undo) pair) and a request that must be serialised for replay or multiprocessing, because lambdas and locally defined closures cannot be pickled while module-level callables and classes can.
code_sketch:
import functools

class InsertText:
    def __init__(self, doc, pos, text): self.doc, self.pos, self.text = doc, pos, text
    def __call__(self): self.doc.insert(self.pos, self.text)   # callable = command
    def undo(self): self.doc.delete(self.pos, len(self.text))

history.append(InsertText(doc, 0, "x"))
history[-1]()                        # invoker runs the command
history.pop().undo()                 # inverse travels with the command

insert = functools.partial(doc.insert, 0, "x")   # parameters without a class
pitfalls: Bound methods and closures hold strong references to their receivers, so an undo history pins documents, frames and large payloads - trim entries or hold weak references.

Lambdas and nested functions cannot be pickled, so a command log meant for replay or multiprocessing must use module-level functions or classes; functools.partial is picklable only when its func and args are.
Late-binding closures and mutable default arguments capture shared state, so a replayed command applies today's parameters instead of the recorded ones unless the current value is bound explicitly.
The GIL is not a substitute for correctness: a shared history still needs a lock and a single owner of the invoker.
